cells.tense: You are the turning now, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.ask: Name one thing arriving this week and one thing you're done with. Say both out loud — to yourself or to someone — then let the ending close and stay open to the next.
cells.core:
A door opens, a chapter ends, and you meet it. That is not a mood you happen to be in today. It is how this capacity is running right now, and it shows in how you handle endings: you let things finish.

What makes it work is that you do not cling to the closing. A cycle ends and you are already open to the next one arriving, which is rarer than it sounds. This balance asks something of you. Keep saying yes to what is next, not only goodbye to what is done. Meet the arrival, release the grip, and the freshness stays yours.
cells.sheetLine: You meet what arrives and let what ends end.
cells.place: at the threshold where something is let go

cells.tense: You are living ahead of the moment, bracing for a door not yet opened.
cells.ask: When the next ending comes, wait one day before responding. Notice the urge to decide the whole next chapter early, and let that day be enough.
cells.core:
With your feet on today, this looks like handling the ending in front of you and letting the next one wait its turn. The pen is in your hand and you are using it here.

Instead you have already decided how the next thing goes, and you are living in that version. The turning is not yours to steer anymore — it carries you. You call it fate, or timing, or just how things go, and from where you stand the cause sits somewhere else. The same endings arrive over and over because the one in front of you has not been met. You are bracing at a future you cannot write in, and the present keeps slipping past the way it has. Meeting it starts with not deciding ahead of it.
cells.sheetLine: The current is carrying you. You stopped choosing.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been holding past its end. Write down what it gave you, then tell one person it's finished for you. No ceremony, just the saying.
cells.core:
The threshold works as a place you step through. The thing ends, you let it end, and the space it clears belongs to you.

What is happening instead: you stopped at some threshold and did not quite come through. The turning keeps happening around you, but you keep your back to it — as if staying still kept something from ending, or as if arriving fully here would mean leaving something behind. What you left is not being preserved. It is just not being released. Letting go has come to look like loss, so you hold. The grip feels safe, and it is holding you at the edge of the freshness on the other side. Letting one done thing close is how the release starts working again — not by pushing yourself through the door.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping what's finished. It isn't finished.

cells.tense: You are writing in a room you don't know you're in.
cells.ask: Pick one result that surprised you this month. Trace back the choice that produced it and say, out loud, that you made it. One result, one choice, said plainly.
cells.core:
At its best this looks like standing at the turning and knowing you are the one turning — the ending is yours to make, the arrival is yours to meet, and your hand is in both.

What is happening instead: things turn and you are somewhere else when they do. The ending arrives, the new thing starts, and it looks like it happened to you. Outcomes follow from your own choices and surprise you anyway. The turning is running; you are just not claiming it. The release you call luck, or timing, or other people's decisions is yours to name. Say one choice out loud as yours and the wheel you did not know you were on becomes something you can steer.
cells.sheetLine: You're choosing this. You haven't said so yet.
cells.place: at the threshold where something is let go
